demographics: Upper GI bleeding is more common in men

risk_factors.text: Peptic ulcer disease or prior GI bleed

chief_complaints.text: My stool is black and tarry
There is bright red blood in my stool
I have been having dark, loose stools

hpi.onset: Sudden or gradual depending on the source; upper GI bleeding often presents with vomiting blood or black stools, lower GI bleeding with red blood per rectum
hpi.duration: Hours to days for acute bleeding; chronic occult bleeding may be present for weeks
hpi.progression: May stop spontaneously or continue; ongoing bleeding can lead to worsening weakness, dizziness and shock
hpi.location: Upper GI tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum) or lower GI tract (colon, rectum, anus)
hpi.radiation: Pain may radiate to the back or epigastrium if ulcer related; bleeding itself does not radiate
hpi.quality: Vomiting red blood or coffee-ground material; black tarry stools; red blood mixed with or coating stool
hpi.severity: Varies from occult blood loss to massive hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability
relieving: Nothing specific; stopping the offending agent may help
pertinent_negatives: Bright red blood only from the rectum without black stools
No prior history of GI bleeding

atypical.how_it_differs: May present with confusion, falls, or weakness without obvious bleeding signs; less tachycardia and pain.
Often presents with vomiting blood or blood in stool due to swallowed maternal blood, esophagitis, or intussusception; may have irritability and poor feeding.
May present with hyperemesis causing Mallory-Weiss tear or with bleeding from esophageal varices due to pregnancy-related liver changes; symptoms may be attributed to morning sickness.
May have bleeding from CMV or other opportunistic infections, or from medication-related ulcers; fever and systemic symptoms may be present.

general.mild: Alert, comfortable, no distress; normal color
general.moderate: Mildly pale, mild anxiety, able to converse
general.severe: Pale, diaphoretic, anxious, restless, appears unwell
general.critical: Markedly pale or mottled, lethargic or confused, cold clammy extremities, near-syncopal

labs.caveat: May be normal early in acute bleeding before hemodilution; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude significant blood loss.
Falls with resuscitation and hemodilution; trend is more useful than a single value.
Thrombocytopenia suggests cirrhosis with portal hypertension or a primary hematologic problem.
Elevated by warfarin, liver disease, or vitamin K deficiency; guides reversal.
Prolonged by heparin or a coagulopathy.
A BUN/creatinine ratio above 30 suggests an upper GI source from absorbed blood.
Rises with hypovolemia and prerenal injury; affects contrast and medication dosing.
Low MCV suggests chronic iron deficiency from occult blood loss.
Low ferritin supports chronic blood loss; may be normal or high in acute inflammation.
Elevated lactate marks hypoperfusion and risk of decompensation.
Elevated in alcohol-related liver disease or ischemic hepatitis.
Elevated bilirubin suggests cirrhosis or hemolysis.
Low albumin supports chronic liver disease.
Negative. Required in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or endoscopy; rules out pregnancy-related bleeding.

findings.finding: Diffuse ST depression or T-wave flattening from demand ischemia in severe anemia
Nonspecific ST-T changes in the setting of anemia or electrolyte disturbance

Detects coagulopathy or anticoagulant effect that must be corrected

Localizes and treats an upper GI source
initial.only_if: suspected upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena, or high BUN/creatinine ratio)

confirmatory.why: Definitive diagnosis and therapy for lower GI bleeding

supporting.test: CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
supporting.why: Localizes active bleeding when endoscopy is nondiagnostic or the patient is unstable
supporting.only_if: Localizes active bleeding when endoscopy is nondiagnostic or the patient is unstable

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Does not evaluate GI bleeding; used only to exclude a urinary source

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT or endoscopy in anyone who could be pregnant
Resuscitate and stabilize before endoscopy in massive bleeding
Upper endoscopy first for hematemesis or melena; colonoscopy first for hematochezia in a stable patient
Reverse anticoagulation or coagulopathy before or during endoscopy when bleeding is severe

differential.name: Peptic ulcer disease
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of upper GI bleeding; presents with hematemesis, melena, or both, often with epigastric pain.
differential.trigger: Epigastric pain with NSAID use or prior ulcer history, plus hematemesis or melena

history: Epigastric burning pain relieved or worsened by food
Prior ulcer or H. pylori infection
exam: No stigmata of chronic liver disease
labs: Elevated BUN/creatinine ratio suggesting an upper source
Anemia with acute or chronic blood loss
imaging: Gastric or duodenal ulcer with active bleeding or a visible vessel on EGD

differential.name: Esophageal or gastric varices
differential.why_considered: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis can cause sudden, massive upper GI bleeding that looks like a severe ulcer bleed.
differential.trigger: Known cirrhosis, heavy alcohol use, or signs of chronic liver disease with hematemesis

imaging: Esophageal or gastric varices on EGD
Signs of portal hypertension on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Mallory-Weiss tear
differential.why_considered: Vomiting blood after forceful retching or vomiting, often after alcohol use, mimics other upper GI bleeding sources.

history: Forceful vomiting or retching before hematemesis
exam: Usually no epigastric tenderness or chronic liver stigmata
imaging: Linear mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction on EGD

differential.name: Diverticular bleeding
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of lower GI bleeding in older adults; presents with sudden, painless hematochezia.

history: Sudden, painless passage of large amounts of red or maroon blood
exam: Bright red blood on digital rectal exam
imaging: Diverticula with stigmata of recent bleeding on colonoscopy
Active contrast extravasation on CT angiography if bleeding is ongoing

differential.name: Colorectal cancer
differential.why_considered: Can present with occult or overt lower GI bleeding, especially in older adults with iron deficiency anemia or changed bowel habits.
differential.trigger: Iron deficiency anemia, weight loss, or a change in bowel habits in an older adult

history: Family history of colorectal cancer or polyps
exam: Occult or visible blood on digital rectal exam
labs: Iron deficiency anemia with low MCV and ferritin
imaging: Colonic mass or stricture on colonoscopy

differential.name: Ischemic colitis
differential.why_considered: Presents with lower abdominal pain and hematochezia in older adults, often with vascular risk factors.

history: Abrupt crampy lower abdominal pain followed by urgency to defecate
Older age with atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, or hypotension
imaging: Segmental colonic wall thickening on CT
Mucosal edema, erythema, or ulceration on colonoscopy

differential.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
differential.why_considered: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease can cause chronic or acute lower GI bleeding with diarrhea and abdominal pain.

exam: Perianal disease or fistulas in Crohn disease
imaging: Continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum in ulcerative colitis
Skip lesions and transmural inflammation in Crohn disease

differential.name: Hemorrhoidal bleeding
differential.why_considered: Bright red blood per rectum, often after defecation, is a common benign cause of lower GI bleeding.

history: Bright red blood on toilet paper or coating the stool
exam: Visible or palpable hemorrhoids on rectal exam
labs: Usually normal hemoglobin unless chronic bleeding

severity.mild: Occult or small-volume bleeding with normal vital signs and minimal or no anemia; patient is alert and comfortable.
severity.moderate: Visible bleeding with mild tachycardia or orthostatic changes, mild pallor, and moderate anemia; patient is hemodynamically stable but symptomatic.
severity.severe: Ongoing or large-volume bleeding with resting tachycardia, hypotension, marked pallor, and significant anemia; patient may be anxious or restless.
severity.critical: Massive hemorrhage with shock, altered mental status, cool clammy extremities, and severe anemia; requires immediate resuscitation and urgent intervention.

red_flags.meaning: Upper GI bleeding; requires urgent endoscopy and resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Melena or hematochezia with hemodynamic instability
red_flags.meaning: Significant ongoing blood loss; resuscitate and localize source urgently

red_flags.finding: Systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg or heart rate above 120
red_flags.meaning: Shock from blood loss; immediate fluid and blood resuscitation
Possible variceal bleed; high mortality, needs urgent endoscopic therapy

special_populations.differences: May present with confusion, falls, or weakness without obvious bleeding signs; less tachycardia and pain; higher mortality and more comorbid conditions.
Often presents with vomiting blood or blood in stool due to swallowed maternal blood, esophagitis, or intussusception; may have irritability and poor feeding; NSAID use and cirrhosis are uncommon.

May present with hyperemesis causing Mallory-Weiss tear or with bleeding from esophageal varices due to pregnancy-related liver changes; symptoms may be attributed to morning sickness; pregnancy test required before imaging.
May have bleeding from CMV or other opportunistic infections, or from medication-related ulcers; fever and systemic symptoms may be present; consider infectious causes.
Uremia can cause platelet dysfunction and bleeding; also at higher risk from anticoagulants and NSAIDs; careful medication dosing and reversal.
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension increases risk of variceal bleeding and coagulopathy; requires aggressive reversal and specific therapy.

key_questions.question: What did the blood look like — did you vomit red blood or coffee-ground material?
key_questions.looking_for: Hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis localizes the source to the upper GI tract

key_questions.question: What color are your stools — black and tarry, maroon, or bright red?
key_questions.looking_for: Melena suggests an upper source; hematochezia suggests a lower source (or a brisk upper bleed)

key_questions.question: When did the bleeding start, and is it still going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Ongoing bleeding with instability requires urgent resuscitation and endoscopy

key_questions.question: How much blood have you seen — a few drops, a cupful, or more?
key_questions.looking_for: Estimates volume lost and guides triage and transfusion needs

key_questions.question: Do you have abdominal pain, and where is it?
key_questions.looking_for: Epigastric pain suggests ulcer; painless bleeding suggests diverticular or variceal source

key_questions.question: Have you felt lightheaded, dizzy on standing, or fainted?
Have you had any forceful vomiting or retching before the blood appeared?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests a Mallory-Weiss tear at the gastroesophageal junction

key_questions.question: Have you had black stools or a positive stool test before?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior GI bleeding or chronic occult blood loss

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of ulcers, liver disease, or diverticulosis?
key_questions.looking_for: Peptic ulcer disease, cirrhosis with varices, or diverticular disease as the source

key_questions.question: Do you take NSAIDs, aspirin, or blood thinners?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs and antithrombotics cause ulcers and worsen bleeding; anticoagulants require reversal

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy use raises risk of varices, gastritis, and Mallory-Weiss tear

key_questions.question: Have you had unintentional weight loss or a change in bowel habits?
key_questions.looking_for: Suggests colorectal cancer as the bleeding source

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last menstrual period?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes pregnancy-related bleeding and is required before imaging or endoscopy

key_questions.question: Any blood in your urine or vaginal bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Excludes a urinary or gynecologic source of the blood

reasoning_points: Localizes the source as upper or lower GI based on hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia
Identifies risk factors such as NSAID use, alcohol, cirrhosis, or anticoagulation
Assesses hemodynamic stability and severity of blood loss
Recognizes an elevated BUN/creatinine ratio as suggesting an upper GI source
Excludes pregnancy before imaging or endoscopy
Selects EGD for suspected upper bleeding and colonoscopy for suspected lower bleeding
Considers must-not-miss causes: peptic ulcer, varices, and colorectal cancer
Plans resuscitation, transfusion, and reversal of coagulopathy when indicated

easy: Classic hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis with melena
Known peptic ulcer disease or NSAID use
Anemia with an elevated BUN/creatinine ratio
medium: Older adult with painless hematochezia from diverticular bleeding
Patient on warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant
Normal hemoglobin early in acute bleeding
hard: Older adult presenting with confusion, falls, or weakness without obvious bleeding
Occult bleeding with iron deficiency anemia and no visible blood
Brisk upper GI bleed presenting as hematochezia
Cirrhotic patient with variceal bleeding and coagulopathy
Pregnant patient with bleeding attributed to morning sickness
